name: Edomae-zushi (Edo-style nigiri and its akazu shari)
text: Edo-period nigiri sushi, traditionally credited to Hanaya Yohei, who is said to have perfected it and to have seasoned his rice with akazu (red vinegar from sake lees). One source titles Ryogoku as its birthplace. Accounts of Yohei's own practice vary by source, and the 'real Edomae uses akazu' idea is described as handed down later. After the war, many shops moved from akazu to rice vinegar.
flavor: Akazu shari reads as rounder, with umami and some sweetness; shiro (rice-vinegar) shari is cleaner and sharper.
use: Nigiri of marinated, cured and fresh neta on vinegared rice; choice of vinegar is a house style decision.
craft: The sources found give no standard ratio of vinegar, sugar and salt to rice, and shops differ, so verify any ratio in-house rather than copying one. One explanation is that akazu's own sweetness and umami let early shops skip sugar, which was then costly.
src: The Gate: Ryogoku origin of Edomae sushi
Pocket Concierge: akashari vs shirozushi and Edomae history

name: Akashari and shiro-shari (red and white sushi rice)
text: Akashari is sushi rice seasoned with akazu, the sake-lees vinegar that spread in the late Edo period when rice was precious and rice vinegar was costly. Shiro-shari uses rice vinegar, which became the norm after the war. Sources describe akazu as carrying umami and sweetness, so sugar could be left out; no common standard ratio was found.
flavor: Akashari: amber tint, deeper and rounder. Shiro-shari: white, clean, brighter acidity.
use: Choose by neta: the sources frame it as a style choice between the Edo tradition and the postwar rice-vinegar norm.
craft: Because no published standard exists, judge each blend by tasting it with the neta and by how the grains hold. Do not assume a quoted ratio is authoritative.
src: Hamazon Special: akazu vs rice vinegar
Sushidou: making shari and its history

name: Kakinoha-zushi of Chizu (Tottori)
text: MAFF lists this kakinoha-zushi as a regional dish of Chizu town in Tottori. It is described as devised inland to preserve salted trout, and is eaten on festival days, at New Year and when entertaining guests. The sushi is wrapped in persimmon leaf, as in the better-known Nara version.
flavor: Salted trout over vinegared rice, with persimmon leaf aroma.
use: Festive and hospitality food (hare no hi); a preserved sushi that keeps during the wrapping rest.
craft: The fish is salt-cured first, so judge the salt level of the fish against the shari's seasoning; the sources give no figures.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Kakinoha-zushi, Tottori

name: Kakinoha-zushi of Wakayama
text: MAFF records Wakayama's kakinoha-zushi as once an indispensable food of autumn festivals (hare-shoku). Today it is made all year with a variety of toppings. It is a persimmon-leaf-wrapped pressed sushi, listed separately from the Nara and Tottori versions.
flavor: Vinegared rice and topping carrying persimmon leaf aroma.
use: Festival and gift sushi; now sold and eaten throughout the year.
craft: MAFF notes the shift from a seasonal festival dish to year-round variety; a professional should check whether a given product is salted mackerel or another topping.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Kakinoha-zushi, Wakayama

name: Saba no hako-zushi (Izu, Shizuoka)
text: A box-pressed mackerel sushi from the Izu area, made on festival and other special days (hare no hi). MAFF notes it began as fishermen's food, so it uses locally caught mackerel.
flavor: Mackerel pressed over vinegared rice.
use: Festival dish of Izu; cut from the pressed block.
craft: The sources give no process figures; the point to note is the local-catch tradition, so check the mackerel's freshness and cure.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Saba no hako-zushi, Shizuoka

name: Saba-zushi of Hyogo
text: MAFF describes Hyogo's traditional saba-zushi as using vinegar-cured salted mackerel, in several forms: whole-fish (sugata) sushi, bar (bo) sushi and nigiri. The form varies, but the mackerel is salted and then vinegar-cured before it meets the rice.
flavor: Cured, tangy mackerel on seasoned rice.
use: Served sliced from a bar, whole-fish style, or as nigiri.
craft: Salting then vinegar cure is the defining step; the page gives no timings, so set them by fish size and fat.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Saba-zushi, Hyogo

name: Tekone-zushi (Mie)
text: MAFF lists tekone-zushi as a dish of the Ise-Shima food area of Mie. The name is explained as coming from fishermen who filleted the catch on the boat and mixed it by hand (te-kone). It mainly uses red-fleshed fish, namely bonito and tuna.
flavor: Seasoned red-fleshed fish mixed through vinegared rice.
use: Fishermen's mixed sushi; the fish is combined with the rice by hand.
craft: Because the fish is mixed in, handle the red fish cleanly and cold; the source gives no marinade or ratio.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Tekone-zushi, Mie

name: Nare-zushi of Mie (nama-nare)
text: MAFF describes nare-zushi as a preserved food in which salted fish and rice undergo lactic fermentation. Mie's version is a 'nama-nare' in which the rice is also eaten, unlike the 'hon-nare' typified by Shiga's funa-zushi.
flavor: Sour from lactic fermentation; the rice is part of the dish.
use: Preserved fermented sushi eaten with its rice.
craft: The hon-nare/nama-nare distinction is the key: nama-nare is eaten earlier and with its rice. The sources seen give no salt ratio or duration.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Nare-zushi, Mie
MAFF Nippon dento shoku zukan: Nare-zushi

name: Sasa-zushi of Niigata
text: Eaten mainly around Joetsu. MAFF contrasts it with Ishikawa's sasa-zushi, which is vinegared rice wrapped in bamboo grass and pressed. Niigata's is built on a kumazasa leaf: rice laid on the leaf, then toppings and condiments arranged on top.
flavor: Open, arranged toppings on seasoned rice, with bamboo-grass aroma.
use: Served on the leaf as an arranged sushi, not pressed.
craft: Do not confuse the two sasa-zushi: Ishikawa presses wrapped rice, Niigata arranges toppings on the leaf.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Sasa-zushi, Niigata

name: Iizushi of Niigata (Murakami nare-zushi)
text: MAFF's Niigata listing presents iizushi as a traditional nare-zushi of Murakami. As a fermented rice-and-fish sushi it belongs to the narezushi family; the search summary did not carry process figures, which should be read from the MAFF page itself.
flavor: Fermented and tangy, as nare-zushi.
use: Traditional preserved sushi of the Murakami area.
craft: Check the MAFF page for fish, salt and fermentation details before quoting any figure; none were available in the material gathered here.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Iizushi, Niigata

name: Sanma-zushi of Totsukawa (Nara)
text: MAFF lists sanma-zushi mainly as a regional dish of Totsukawa village, Yoshino district, Nara. Salted sanma is soaked in vinegar and laid on vinegared rice, then wrapped and left to settle. Fewer people make it at home now; it is sold at roadside stations and farm shops.
flavor: Vinegar-cured, salted sanma on rice.
use: Wrapped sushi sold locally; rested before eating.
craft: Salt, then vinegar soak, then rest: the sequence matters. The page summary gave no timings.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Sanma-zushi, Nara

name: Inaka-zushi (Kochi)
text: A Kochi regional nigiri-style sushi whose toppings are vegetables rather than seafood. The account given is that it began when kelp and nori were hard to obtain, so mountain ingredients were used.
flavor: Vegetable-forward, mild.
use: Home and regional sushi using mountain ingredients.
craft: Because no fish is involved, the quality rests on the rice seasoning and the preparation of each vegetable; no specifics were in the summary seen.

name: Iwakuni-zushi (Yamaguchi)
text: A pressed sushi also called Tonosama-zushi, from the tradition that it was presented to the Iwakuni lord Kikkawa. MAFF describes it as layered in three to five tiers with ingredients typical of the castle town, such as vinegared Iwakuni lotus root and simmered conger eel.
flavor: Layered, sweet-sour, with lotus root texture.
use: Pressed in a frame and cut; a formal dish.
craft: Layering of three to five tiers is the structure; the lotus root is vinegared separately.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Iwakuni-zushi, Yamaguchi

name: Imogara-iri futomaki-zushi (Yamanashi)
ja: いもがら入り太巻き寿司
text: MAFF lists this as a prefecture-wide dish of Yamanashi: a thick rolled sushi that includes dried imogara, the dried taro stem. It is a home and festival roll in the thick-roll family.
flavor: Chewy dried taro stem inside rolled rice.
use: Cut thick rolls for gatherings.
craft: Imogara must be rehydrated and seasoned before rolling; the summary gave no details.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Imogara-iri futomaki, Yamanashi

name: Bara no hana futomaki-zushi (Chiba)
ja: ばらの花の太巻き寿司
text: A decorative thick roll of Chiba, listed in MAFF's regional cooking series. It is noted for a showy appearance and as easy for parent and child to make together; MAFF's recipe is mirrored on Cookpad.
flavor: Mild, vinegared rice with a pattern in cross-section.
use: Festive roll, cut to show the rose pattern.
craft: The pattern is set at rolling; cut with a clean wet blade.
src: MAFF recipe on Cookpad: Bara no hana futomaki

name: Sasanishiki
text: A light, low-stickiness table rice. The sources describe it as clean and without harshness, and say it suits vinegared rice for rolls. Growers have been declining in number.
flavor: Light, clean, little stickiness.
use: Cited as suited to sushi rice and norimaki.
craft: Low stickiness means the grains separate easily; test cooking water and vinegar at your own ratio, as no figures were found.

name: Tsuyahime
text: A Yamagata-bred rice valued for white, glossy cooked grains. It is less sticky than Koshihikari, with a lighter texture. In a 2024-crop planted-area ranking on a private site it placed 11th at 1.5%.
flavor: Bright white, glossy, light with modest stickiness.
use: Table rice; its stickiness is lower than Koshihikari.
craft: Compare with Koshihikari for water; the sources give no cooking ratios.

name: Yumepirika
text: A Hokkaido rice with low amylose, giving a markedly sticky, soft texture. A private ranking site puts it 8th by 2024-crop planted area at 1.8%.
flavor: Soft, sticky, mochi-like.
use: Table rice for those who like softness.
craft: Low amylose rice suits stickiness-first uses; for sushi rice, test grain separation.

name: Nanatsuboshi
text: Hokkaido's mainstay variety. It tolerates cold, has good eating quality, and is described as number one in Hokkaido for both production and consumption. It ranks 5th by planted area at 3.4% in a 2024-crop private ranking.
flavor: Balanced, good eating quality.
use: Everyday table rice in Hokkaido.
craft: Cold tolerance is the agronomic point; no sushi-specific data in the sources.

name: Uonuma Koshihikari
text: Koshihikari grown in the Uonuma region of southern Niigata, which covers Uonuma, Minami-Uonuma, Tokamachi, Ojiya, Yuzawa and Tsunan. Sellers credit snowmelt water, mineral soil and large day-night temperature gaps. It has frequently won the top 'Toku-A' taste rating; the number of Toku-A years differs by seller claim, so check the official record.
flavor: Sweet and sticky, keeps texture when cooled.
use: Premium table rice and a benchmark brand.
craft: Distinguish 'Uonuma' from 'Minami-Uonuma' on labels; verify origin and year of the Toku-A rating.

name: Ittou-mai (first-grade rice)
text: Grade under the agricultural product inspection of brown rice. For non-glutinous brown rice, first grade needs at least 70% well-formed grains, moisture of 15% or less (one source lists a 16.0% limit), and damaged, dead, colored, foreign grain and impurities totalling 15% or less. Dead rice 7% or less, colored 0.1%, husk 0.3%. Second grade needs 60% well-formed. Preliminary 2025 crop results: 75.6% first, 19.5% second.
flavor: Spoken as 'ittou-mai'; denotes appearance, not flavor.
use: Used on rice trade and labels as a quality baseline.
craft: It is a visual grading of brown rice and says nothing about eating quality; do not equate it with taste.

name: Toku-A (Special A taste rating)
text: The top rating in the taste ranking by the Japan Grain Inspection Association. Uonuma Koshihikari is repeatedly cited with it, but the exact count of years varies between seller pages and should be checked.
flavor: Read 'toku-ee'.
use: A marketing and purchasing signal.
craft: It rates a given crop year and area, not the variety forever; confirm the year.

name: Rice planted-area ranking (2024 crop)
text: A private ranking for the 2024 crop gives Hitomebore 2nd (8.4%), Akitakomachi 4th (6.7%), Nanatsuboshi 5th (3.4%), Yumepirika 8th (1.8%) and Tsuyahime 11th (1.5%). Another source calls Hinohikari the third most planted. It is secondary data and has not been checked against MAFF statistics.
flavor: Market-share style table.
use: Gauges how common a variety is.
craft: Check MAFF statistics before quoting shares.
